data.title: EU’s new pharma package an “opportunity missed” industry says
data.description:
A new set of rules designed to boost European pharmaceutical competitiveness has been given the parliamentary green light, though reception by the industry has been lukewarm.

On 25 November, the European Parliament approved long-awaited reforms to the EU’s pharmaceutical legislation. The package, which has been in the legislative process for nearly four years, is designed to prevent medicine shortages, boost industry innovation, and combat antimicrobial resistance.The parliament did not provide a timeline for enforcement of the provisions.

It marks the first full overhaul of the continent’s pharmaceutical legislation in two decades, with experts placing weight on its ability to turn Europe’s competitive fortunes around. In an open letter, the CEOs of many of Europe’s large pharmaceutical companies have said the region has fallen behind both the US and China across a variety of measures such as medicine innovation and commercial opportunity.

The European Federation of Pharmaceutical Industries and Associations (EFPIA) praised the package for retaining data protection duration, regulatory assessment streamlining, and the priority medicine scheme. It also highlighted regulatory sandboxes for new technologies and new antimicrobial incentives.  However, the trade body asserted that the legislation does not fully meet the mark.

“Given that the legislation is set to underpin the next two decades of European pharmaceutical innovation, it falls short on some key aspects. In its entirety, [the legislation] will not be strong enough to move the needle on European competitiveness in a meaningful way,” the trade body said in a statement.

Medicines for Europe director Adrian van den Hoven was more positive, saying: “[Wednesday’s] adoption marks an important milestone for patient access and medicine security of supply. We will engage with stakeholders and the EU to deliver on their promises: equitable access to medicines for patients across Europe, timely competition and health security for Europe.”

One of the most important aspects is the European Commission’s (EC) desire to reduce dependency on non-EU countries for medicines. This comes at a time when pharma imports and exports are under the spotlight given tariffs and drug pricing reforms under the Trump administration in the US. Wider geopolitical events also mean governments are moving to bolster local supply chains.

As part of the new legislation to incentivise EU-based manufacturing, suppliers will be rewarded proportionally to the share of their medicinal products and active pharmaceutical substances manufactured in the EU.

EU countries will also be able to require companies to supply medicines in sufficient quantities to meet patients’ needs. To support earlier market entry of generic medicines, manufacturers will be allowed to conduct certain activities during the original product’s market protection period. A maximum protection period of 11 years for newly authorised medicines is set out in the rules, with eight of those carrying data protection.

Bastien Pavec, senior associate at Clifford Chance, told Pharmaceutical Technology: “The EU Pharma Package includes several long-awaited measures to support innovation, from shorter authorisation procedures and regulatory sandboxes to incentives for new antimicrobials. Yet, it does not fundamentally reshape Europe’s regulatory framework. New launch provisions, a broader Bolar exemption and additional medicine-shortage obligations will create further complexity and also uncertainties, but will ultimately lead to a more robust European playing field.”

EC president Ursula von der Leyen wants to make Europe the most attractive place for life sciences by 2030. She is also overseeing the implementation of the Biotech Act, a framework designed to close the innovation and funding gap to global rivals by boosting the biotech and biomanufacturing sectors.  

Big pharma has called for rapid policy change in Europe to maintain the flow of capital into the continent. In addition to the open letter in September, there was a separate one from 32 CEOs of both US and European companies to EC President Ursula von der Leyen requesting new legislation.

Pavec added: “[The EU] reforms fall short of the major competitiveness shift many had hoped for. They nevertheless send a clear signal: life sciences truly is a priority for EU institutions, and more should be expected to come. The forthcoming EU Biotech Act may prove to close an important gap, particularly if it can deliver a genuinely more competitive regulatory environment.”

But the EC’s strategy comes as both the US and China also ramp up their respective pharmaceutical industries. Big pharma has invested hundreds of billions to bolster manufacturing in the US after being threatened with heavy levies, while China has laid out a roadmap to increase its exports of innovative drugs.

Nathalie Moll, Director General of EFPIA, said: “At a time when Europe continues to fall behind the US and China in pharmaceutical R&D, clinical trials and manufacturing, this important opportunity to help Europe compete has largely been missed. 

“Looking ahead, Europe needs ambitious, strategic, long-term policies on par with those seen in the US and China. The Biotech Act is a great place to start. This should be complemented with a strategic dialogue on life sciences.”

data.title: German PEI approves two Stallergenes’ allergy therapies for paediatric use
data.description:
Germany’s Paul-Ehrlich-Institut (PEI) has approved paediatric indication extensions for Stallergenes Greer’s Staloral 3 Trees and Staloral Birch sublingual allergen immunotherapy (SLIT) treatments.

The decision permits children and adolescents aged 5 to 17 years with tree pollen-induced allergic conjunctivitis or allergic rhino conjunctivitis (ARC), with or without controlled allergic asthma, to receive these liquid immunotherapy treatments. Both therapies are already available in the country for adults.

Stallergenes Greer commercialises the two products across 21 countries according to local regulatory statuses.

The approvals were backed by the multinational Phase IIIb YOBI clinical trial (NCT05668390 and EudraCT 2022-002012-23), conducted across 64 sites in 12 European countries.

The randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study evaluated daily 300 IR Staloral Birch against placebo over two consecutive pollen seasons in 553 patients aged 5 to 17 years with moderate-to-severe birch pollen-induced ARC.

Primary endpoint was met, showing a statistically significant 41.7% improvement in the ARC total combined score against placebo during the second season.

Safety outcomes aligned with the established profile of 300 IR Birch liquid immunotherapy. The findings also validate the paediatric expansion for Staloral 3 Trees, which covers alder, birch, and hazel within the homologous group.

Stallergenes Greer chief medical officer Dr Silvia Scurati said: “Advancing allergy care for younger patients is central to us and these paediatric indication extensions are an important step forward.

“For young patients with birch-group pollen allergy, symptoms can come back season after season and weigh on everyday life.

“Based on the YOBI study of Staloral Birch, these extensions bring Staloral Birch and Staloral 3 Trees, liquid sublingual immunotherapies already authorised in adults, to children and adolescents in Germany.”

Headquartered in Baar, Switzerland, Stallergenes Greer provides human and veterinary allergen immunotherapies across 46 countries globally.

data.title: Hetero starts lenacapavir rollout for HIV prevention in Africa
data.description:
Pharmaceutical manufacturer Hetero has begun phased shipments of lenacapavir to Africa for the prevention of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), dispatching an initial batch of 300,000 vials across Uganda, Zambia, and Zimbabwe.

The rollout of the generic injectable places the company among the first globally to distribute a generic version of the twice-yearly preventive medicine.

The World Health Organization (WHO) has recommended lenacapavir as an additional pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) option after trials showed it to be highly effective at lowering the HIV transmission risk.

Hetero anticipates release of its generic oral initiation tablets by January 2027 to provide the full regimen alongside the injection.

Until that time, Gilead Sciences will continue to supply the oral starter tablets needed before beginning injections, subject to national requirements.

Hetero Group of Companies managing director Dr Vamsi Krishna Bandi said: “The launch of generic lenacapavir in Africa is a moment of immense pride for Hetero, as we prepare to mark 30 years of championing the cause of expanding access to critical, life-saving medicines across the continent.

“With lenacapavir, the next decade presents an extraordinary opportunity to avert new HIV infections on a scale that could reshape Africa’s public-health future.  Our vertically integrated manufacturing capabilities have been central to that commitment, enabling us to bring quality, affordability and scale together.

“With an annual production capacity of 15 million vials of generic lenacapavir and the ability to expand further, we are ready to support wider access to HIV prevention across Africa.”

The deliveries follow non-exclusive voluntary licensing agreements signed by Gilead Sciences with six generic manufacturers, allowing the production and distribution of generic lenacapavir across 120 eligible countries.

In September 2025, Hetero partnered with the Gates Foundation involving upfront funding and volume guarantees to accelerate production and provide active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) to other generic manufacturers.

Procurement is supported through the Global Fund’s expert review panel (ERP) mechanism, which issued recommendations for both the injectable formulation and oral initiation tablets.

In Zimbabwe, the medicine is being procured through the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) using Global Fund financing.

Hetero plans to supply 10 additional African nations in early 2027 and introduce the generic drug in India over coming months, subject to regulatory clearances.

data.title: First on-demand pill for hereditary angioedema attacks recommended for NHS use
data.description:
In the same month Chiesi closed its $1.9bn acquisition of rare disease specialist KalVista, the Italian drugmaker has secured a regulatory win in the UK for the asset that formed the centrepiece of the transaction.

The UK’s National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) has issued a positive decision for Ekterly (sebetralstat), recommending the drug’s use on the National Health Service (NHS) for patients with hereditary angioedema (HAE).

As per Ekterly’s label, it will be used for the treatment of HAE attacks in adult and adolescent patients aged 12 years and older. The final draft recommendation marks a U-turn from an initial refusal via a provisional decision made in October 2025.

As per the UK’s reimbursement framework, the NHS now has 90 days to roll out the treatment to patients.  

HAE is a rare genetic disease that causes unpredictable, painful attacks of tissue swelling in various locations of the body that can be life-threatening depending on the area affected. According to research, up to 1,500 people in the UK are estimated to be affected by the condition.

KalVista’s Phase III KONFIDENT study (NCT05259917) demonstrated that Ekterly helped patients reach symptom relief following an attack more than five hours faster than placebo. The treatment works by blocking plasma kallikrein, which in turn reduces the amount of bradykinin made during an attack. Bradykinin causes blood vessels to widen and become leaky, allowing fluid to build up in the surrounding tissues, and is the underlying protein that drives attacks.

In its appraisal, NICE said the drug provides benefits and value for money, allowing its routine use across the NHS. The agency highlighted advantages such as medication convenience and easier self-administration over injectable treatments.

KalVista’s pill, which is approved in the UK, Europe, and the US, among other regions, represents a major advancement in treatment options for the genetic swelling disorder. Unlike BioCryst’s Orladeyo (berotralstat hydrochloride), which is taken daily for prophylaxis, Ekterly is administered following the onset of symptoms, offering patients an on-demand treatment. There are a range of drugs for acute treatment, though these are all injectable, unlike KalVista’s oral option.

HAE has traditionally been treated with these injections that either counter an attack or are administered in a preventative manner. In 2025, there were two new injections approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) – CSL Behring’s Andembry (garadacimab-gxii) and Ionis Pharmaceuticals’ Dawnzera (donidalorsen). These FDA nods came after four years of regulatory dormancy for HAE in the US.

The pill’s commercial ceiling caught the interest of Italian pharma company Chiesi. In April 2026, it agreed to buy KalVista for around $1.9bn, representing the largest acquisition in its 90-year history. The deal closed earlier this month.

Ekterly generated $49m in 2025 sales. Chiesi said that bringing the HAE pill on board will help reach its wider 2030 company revenue target of €6bn ($7bn).

data.title: Pharming Group pauses Ruconest manufacturing in US
data.description:
Pharming Group has temporarily paused the manufacturing of Ruconest (C1 esterase inhibitor [recombinant]) and alerted the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on anticipated supply constraints across the country.

The move comes following the failure of a media fill, a standard test that simulates aseptic production procedures, at a third-party fill-finish facility.

Existing inventory of the medicine will maintain availability within mid-December. However, subsequent supplies will depend on resolving the issue, releasing completed batches, and restarting manufacturing.

Output will remain suspended until specialists identify and rectify the root cause of the failure, followed by successful requalification of the manufacturing process.

An investigation into the simulation failure is underway, with the operational timeline and total impact yet to be confirmed. The company stated that it will issue an update once the inquiry is finished.

Supplies of Ruconest already delivered to specialty pharmacies or received by individuals are unaffected by the stoppage and remain suitable for use as directed.

Pharming advised individuals diagnosed with hereditary angioedema (HAE) to consult their healthcare providers to review their management plans.

The business confirmed that the manufacturing incident does not involve any other treatments across its portfolio.

Pharming interim co-CEO and chief commercial officer Leverne Marsh said: “Patients count on Ruconest for acute treatment for HAE, and we take that responsibility seriously.

“Pharming remains committed to supporting continuity of care for patients living with HAE and is working closely with patients, healthcare providers, the Hereditary Angioedema Association (HAEA), and our specialty pharmacy partners to help ensure patients maintain access to appropriate treatment options when they need them most.”

Headquartered in the Netherlands, Pharming Group maintains commercial and operational activities across Europe and the US.

The company concentrates on developing and commercialising therapies for individuals diagnosed with rare genetic and immune disorders.

data.title: Bayer signs $3.25bn oncology deal with Hansoh Pharma
data.description:
Bayer has entered into an exclusive worldwide licensing agreement potentially valued at up to $3.25bn with Hansoh Pharma to develop, manufacture, and commercialise the Phase I oncology candidate HS-20122.

Under the terms of the transaction, Hansoh Pharma will obtain an upfront payment of $150m. The company remains eligible to receive up to $3.1bn in milestone payments linked to clinical development, regulatory approval, and commercialisation, alongside tiered royalties on prospective net sales.

Bayer will obtain commercial and development rights across all global markets excluding the Chinese mainland, Macau, Taiwan, and Hong Kong.

The transaction remains subject to the receipt of required antitrust clearances before taking effect.

Through the agreement, Hansoh Pharma’s antibody–drug conjugate (ADC) programme will be combined with Bayer’s experience in global drug development, manufacturing, and commercialisation infrastructure.

HS-20122 is a bispecific ADC designed to deliver a cytotoxic payload directly to tumours expressing epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) and mesenchymal-epithelial transition factor (c-MET).

Co-expression of these two proteins can contribute to progression of the disease or therapy resistance. The candidate is being developed for solid tumours, including non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC).

Clinical data assessing the safety and efficacy of the ADC in patients with advanced solid tumours, such as NSCLC, were presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology 2026 Congress.

Bayer Pharmaceuticals Division business development and licensing head Juergen Eckhardt said: “We are excited to further advance HS-20122, a next-generation, bispecific ADC, together with Hansoh Pharma.

“Despite treatment advances, people living with lung cancer continue to need new options that offer greater efficacy and improved tolerability.

“This collaboration supports Bayer’s precision oncology strategy by advancing ADCs that more selectively target tumour cells to deliver cancer-killing payloads.”

Last month, Bayer announced plans to invest $2.2bn in a new pharmaceutical manufacturing facility in Ohio, US.

data.title: Cogent Biosciences gains FDA approval for Ekitna combo in GIST
data.description:
The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved Cogent Biosciences’ Ekitna (bezuclastinib) in combination with sunitinib for adult patients with advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumours (GIST) who previously received imatinib.

This decision was supported by findings from the global, randomised Phase III PEAK study (NCT05208047).

The trial assessed the combination of Ekitna and sunitinib against sunitinib monotherapy in individuals with imatinib-resistant or intolerant GIST.

Data collected through the 30 September 2025 cutoff point demonstrated that the combination reduced the disease progression or death risk by 50% compared to monotherapy, yielding a hazard ratio (HR) of 0.50.

Independent central review confirmed a median progression-free survival (PFS) of 16.5 months for the combination versus 9.2 months for sunitinib alone.

Furthermore, 46% of patients receiving the combination therapy achieved an objective response, compared to 26% in the sunitinib comparator group.

Cogent Biosciences president and CEO Andrew Robbins said: “Today’s FDA approval of Ekitna marks an enormous milestone for people living with GIST and a historic milestone for Cogent.

“After seeing the incredible results of the PEAK trial, we were confident this day would come, and we are excited that it is finally here.

“On behalf of all Cogent employees, we are extremely proud to launch Ekitna, which brings new hope to GIST patients searching for better treatment options.”

Following the approval, the company has launched the therapy alongside the Cogent Connect Patient Support Program.

The support scheme aims to help patients and healthcare providers navigate access barriers.

Bezuclastinib functions as a selective tyrosine kinase inhibitor that targets the KIT D816V mutation and other alterations in KIT exon 17.

Cogent Biosciences is also developing targeted therapies directed at mutations in erythroblastic oncogene B2 (ErbB2), Janus kinase 2 (JAK2), kirsten rat sarcoma viral oncogene homolog (KRAS), and phosphoinositide 3-kinase alpha (PI3Kα).

data.title: MAXONA’s MAX-001 secures FDA fast track status for non-opioid pain drug
data.description:
The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has granted fast track designation (FTD) for MAXONA Pharmaceuticals’ oral therapy, MAX-001, a non-opioid drug aimed at treating acute pain.

The regulatory agency provides FTD to support the development and accelerate the review of new therapies that can address unmet medical needs.

This applies to candidates targeting conditions lacking existing treatments or those showing potential advantages, including improved efficacy or positive effects on serious health outcomes.

MAXONA Pharmaceuticals president and CEO Shawn Fatholahi said: “We appreciate the FDA decision to grant fast track status to MAX-001 as a non-opioid oral analgesic for the treatment of acute pain.

“With enrolment in our Phase II trial now underway, the FDA designation will allow us to access the benefits of the fast track programme, which can include more frequent meetings and written communication with the FDA, a rolling review of data submissions and potentially accelerated approval or priority review if conditions are met.

“We look forward to working more closely with the FDA during this important next phase of the MAX-001 clinical development programme.”

The company is evaluating the therapy in the double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled MAX-001 Phase II clinical trial (NCT07937657) involving 276 patients.

The Dental Impaction Pain Model study is assessing the efficacy and safety of multiple MAX-001 doses in patients who are undergoing bilateral impacted mandibular third molar teeth extraction.

This programme follows Phase I testing that concluded in March 2025. It indicated that the therapy was well tolerated with no reported serious or severe adverse events, no related discontinuations, and no abnormal trends across laboratory metrics, ECGs, or vital signs.

Developed as a non-opioid, non-NSAID alternative, MAX-001 is an extended-release nefopam formulation.

Headquartered in Malvern, Pennsylvania, MAXONA Pharmaceuticals is advancing MAX-001 as a new molecular therapy for acute and chronic pain conditions.

There are several companies developing pain medication that is non-opioid-based, including California-based healthcare company Viatris, which inked a billion-dollar deal in October to acquire Pacira BioSciences and its non-opioid pain management therapies.

According to a recent report from GlobalData, 98% of pain medications currently on the market are generics, and neuropathic pain is the largest segment within the pain sector.

data.title: From detecting contamination to predicting risk
data.description:
Facilities can collect samples consistently yet still miss a contamination pathway if the monitoring programme doesn’t reflect how people, materials, and products move through production. For sterile manufacturers, this gap has commercial consequences.

Contamination can put batches at risk of rejection and interrupt production while teams investigate and restore control. Selecting appropriate monitoring locations helps manufacturers direct resources towards the hazards most likely to compromise product quality.

EU good manufacturing practice (GMP) Annex 1 reinforces this preventive approach by requiring a facility-wide contamination control strategy that identifies critical control points and assesses the effectiveness of controls and monitoring. It also makes clear that monitoring or testing alone cannot assure sterility.

Mapping contamination pathways before selecting monitoring locations

Every facility has a different combination of room layouts, equipment, personnel activity and process technologies. A standardised assessment method can bring consistency to decision-making while preserving the detail needed to select locations for an individual site.

Hazard analysis and critical control points (HACCP) can support this process. The approach maps manufacturing activities, identifies hazards and determines where controls and monitoring are needed.

Risk assessments and practical monitoring decisions

A critical control point is a point where applying control is essential to prevent or eliminate a hazard, or reduce it to an acceptable level. The assessment should establish whether existing controls are sufficient and where improvements are needed.

There are several practical questions for identifying suitable monitoring points, including:

  • Which sites do personnel or gloves contact?
  • Where do materials pass from a lower to a higher cleanroom classification?
  • Which areas are difficult to clean and disinfect?
  • Where could airflow patterns allow contamination to accumulate?

These questions help teams examine less obvious vulnerabilities, including equipment guarding, spaces beneath machinery and areas where personnel congregate. Each candidate location needs to be considered in relation to the process and the potential route to product contamination.

Monitoring trends to guide earlier intervention

Once locations are selected, facilities should document where and how sampling will take place. Procedures should establish responsibilities, reporting arrangements and the response to results that require attention. Training makes these decisions repeatable across operators and shifts.

Alert levels and action limits connect data to decisions. Exceeding an action limit should trigger a root cause investigation, product impact assessment and corrective and preventive actions. Alert-level excursions require assessment and follow-up to help avoid further deterioration.

Trending allows microbiologists to examine results in context. A recurring recovery at a particular location or a pattern associated with an operation can prompt closer investigation. Its significance depends on the location, the nature of the contamination and the potential consequences for product and process.

Recognising a drift in environmental quality allows teams to investigate its cause and strengthen controls before the situation worsens. This supports efforts to reduce avoidable batch losses and disruption, although the outcome depends on the effectiveness of the response.

Periodic reassessment should also examine hazards, control effectiveness, sampling frequency and the appropriateness of alert and action levels. As manufacturing activities change, the monitoring rationale needs to remain relevant to the conditions on the production floor.

Supporting risk-based monitoring with appropriate solutions

Putting these decisions into practice requires suitable sampling materials alongside microbiological expertise. Oxoid Remel’s environmental monitoring offering connects culture media and sampling solutions with application guidance. This helps teams consider product selection alongside the contamination pathways, operating conditions, and monitoring objectives specific to their facility.

The portfolio includes Triple Wrap plates in contact and settling formats that come with optional locking lids to ensure an even tighter fit (North America only). Contact plates support surface and personnel monitoring, while settling plates provide an option for monitoring microbial deposition from the air. Available formulations include tryptic soy agar with neutralisers, alongside settling plates without neutralisers, allowing teams to assess the appropriate medium for their sampling conditions.

Oxoid Remel’s Triple Wrap range also includes protective packaging with a vapour-phase hydrogen peroxide barrier layer for isolator workflows. Its deeper-fill settling plates are designed to reduce the risk of the agar drying out, while 2D barcodes support identification and traceability. These features address handling and workflow considerations that sit alongside the selection of monitoring locations.

The task for the microbiology team is to connect these resources to a documented understanding of risk. Each selected location should have a clear purpose, with a rationale explaining the contamination pathway being assessed, the suitability of the sampling method and how the results will inform action. Product selection should support that rationale, with media performance and handling requirements assessed under the facility’s conditions of use.

For manufacturers, the strongest programme continually improves their understanding of risk. Combining appropriate Oxoid Remel sampling solutions with well-chosen locations, consistent procedures and a clear response to emerging trends can help teams generate more useful evidence about environmental control.

data.title: London Life Sciences Week: Dealmaking, AI, and China the talk of the town
data.description:
Black cabs. Red telephone boxes. And more than 5,000 executives and investors from the healthcare industry.

The third week of November marked London Life Sciences Week, during which the capital hosted a plethora of conferences and summits covering various sectors within healthcare.

The GlobalData editorial team attended some of these events, gaining access to panels, fireside chats, and company presentations in biopharma. The team also conducted their own interviews on the sidelines.

Included in this episode are the key themes and takeaways from the Jefferies Global Healthcare Conference, the London Biotech Show, and the inaugural MHRA-DIA Global Summit.

Pharmaceutical editor Robert Barrie, Clinical Trials Arena editor Abigail Beaney, and reporter Annabel Kartal-Allen delve into topics such as dealmaking strategy, China’s biotech policy drive, AI, and rare disease access.

London Life Sciences Week ran from 15-19 November, with this episode recorded on 20 November.
